title: Dual-Role Dynamics in Prompting: Elementary Pre-service Teachers’ AI Prompting Strategies for Representational Choices
extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service elementary teachers prompt generative AI when asked to choose representations for explaining physics ideas in two different roles: as teachers and as students. The authors focus on whether the role a participant adopts changes the way they interact with AI, especially in how explicitly they specify the audience, whether they prescribe a representation type, and how diverse the resulting representations are.

The intervention consisted of two lab-based activities in a physical science course for elementary education majors. In the teacher-role task, participants explained wave velocity to elementary students and used Microsoft Co-Pilot Pro to help generate representations such as pictures, cartoons, analogies, graphs, or activities. In the student-role task, participants explained the Ideal Gas Law to an English teacher and again used AI after first reasoning through the topic. Data came from prompts and AI responses from 20 pre-service elementary teachers at one U.S. university.

The study found that participants were more explicit about the target audience, more prescriptive about the representation, and more likely to generate a wider variety of representations when acting as teachers than when acting as students. When acting as students, prompts were more exploratory and participants more often let AI decide the representation. The authors conclude that role-based prompting patterns may reflect greater agency in teacher mode and suggest that teacher education programs could use AI-supported representation tasks to strengthen science learning and representational competence.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, single-course study with emergent coding and a small sample size (n=20). It is peer-reviewed/academic but does not use a randomized or quasi-experimental design, so evidence strength is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful implications for teacher prompting and representational competence, but it does not measure student achievement or other direct impact outcomes. The observed effects are descriptive and context-specific, so broader impact is unclear.

interventions.use_case: Pre-service elementary teachers used Microsoft Co-Pilot Pro / ChatGPT-style generative AI to help generate representations for explaining wave velocity to elementary students and the Ideal Gas Law to an English teacher.

finding.finding_summary: In a qualitative study of 20 pre-service elementary teachers, AI prompting behavior showed more explicit audience specification, more prescriptive representation requests, and greater representational diversity when participants acted as teachers than when they acted as students. The paper interprets these patterns as evidence of stronger agency and representational competence in the teacher role, but it reports no effect sizes because the analysis was emergent coding rather than a quantitative outcome comparison.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of AI prompts for audience specification, prescriptive vs exploratory wording, and diversity of representations
